title: Detection of Digital Certificates
summary: This detection strategy covers the resource development technique of creating digital certificates, where an adversary builds or obtains a certificate to sign its own tooling so that signed code appears legitimate. It matters because a valid signature on a payload can satisfy trust checks in the operating system and reduce suspicion from users and from some security tools. The telemetry that makes it possible is internal certificate authority issuance logs, certificate transparency logs for public issuance, and endpoint records of signing operations. The main failure mode is that certificate issuance is a normal administrative task, so the rule must separate unusual subjects and non signing hosts from the routine rotation of approved certificates.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for new digital certificates that someone creates, rather than ones that arrive with software. A digital certificate is a file that proves a program or website is genuine. The rule watches the systems that make these certificates and the details written inside them. It catches certificates that copy your own naming style.
beginner.whyItMatters: A certificate that carries a trusted name can make a harmful file look safe. Attackers may copy your company name inside the certificate to gain trust. If you catch the certificate, you can warn about any file signed with it. The same alert also shows which machine is making certificates it should not.
howItWorks: The internal certificate authority, or CA, writes a log line each time it signs a request.
Each line records the subject name, the key usage, the requester, and the issue time.
The SIEM collects these lines together with public certificate transparency records.
The rule compares each new certificate with a baseline of approved names and templates.
It also watches for signing activity on hosts that do not normally sign code.
A certificate with an unusual name or a non signing host raises an alert.
beginner.example: Think of a till receipt at a shop. Each sale prints a receipt with the shop name, the item, and the time. One receipt is worth a look if it shows a product the shop never sells. A receipt from a machine that is not a till is also worth a look. The certificate log is that paper trail.
takeaways: The signal is a new certificate with an unexpected subject or from a non signing host.
Internal authority logs and certificate transparency records together give the full picture.
Watching the request side catches the work before signed files are used.

objectives: Explain how certificate creation helps an attacker appear trustworthy.
Identify certificate authority and transparency logs used for this detection.
Write a rule that flags unusual subjects or requesting hosts.
Explain why baseline knowledge of approved templates is necessary.
Describe the limits of certificate revocation as a response.
dataSources: Internal certificate authority issuance logs recording subject, template, requester identity and issue time
Certificate transparency logs recording public issuance for names that copy organization brands
Sysmon event 13 registry value set for certificate store locations on Windows hosts
Windows Security event 4688 process creation with command line auditing enabled, covering certificate request utilities
logic: The pattern is a certificate being issued or a certificate store being written where the subject name copies a trusted brand, the requesting identity is unexpected, or the host is not part of the code signing group. The fields that must be correlated are the certificate subject and issuer, the template or key usage, the requesting account, the requesting host, and the issue time against the change calendar. The malicious case is a certificate issued to an internal authority for an external sounding subject, or a signing operation on a workstation that has never signed anything. The benign case is the scheduled rotation of an existing server certificate by the team that owns it.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Certificate Issued With Unexpected Subject or Requesting Host
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   service: security
# detection:
#   selection:
#     EventID: 4887
#   filter_known:
#     Subject|contains:
#       - 'CN=Internal Services'
#       - 'CN=Corp Web'
#   condition: selection and not filter_known
# level: medium
falsePositives: Certificate lifecycle automation that renews internal server certificates on a fixed schedule
Test environments that issue short lived self signed certificates for developer sandboxes
Network appliances that request certificates for inspection or management interfaces during deployment
tuningNotes: Export the list of approved subject names, templates, and requesting service accounts from the certificate authority, filter those values inside the rule, and scope alerts to authorities that own production certificates. Baseline issuance per week and per requester so that a sudden rise stands out, and treat any certificate whose subject copies an external brand as high priority. The coverage you lose is an attacker who reuses an approved template and subject on an approved host, so keep an independent review of code signing operations on endpoints.
